title: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva
subtitle: The ageing ladder
objectives: Explain the role of American oak

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Rioja's categories set minimum ageing for reds. Crianza: two years, at least one in barrel. Reserva: three years, at least one in barrel and six months in bottle. Gran Reserva: five years, at least two in barrel and two in bottle. Joven or Genérico wines have little or no barrel age. A coloured seal on the back label shows the category.

steps.title: Oak
steps.body: Rioja's barrels are traditionally 225-litre barricas of American oak, giving vanilla, coconut and dill. Long ageing in old oak gives traditional Rioja its pale colour, mellow fruit and leather. Since the 1990s, many producers use French oak and shorter ageing for darker, fruitier wines. Both styles thrive.

steps.prompt: Order Rioja's categories by minimum ageing, shortest first.
steps.explanation: Each category requires more time in barrel and bottle.

steps.title: The seals
steps.body: Each bottle carries a back-label seal from the Consejo Regulador: green for Crianza, burgundy red for Reserva, blue for Gran Reserva, and white or no barrel indication for Genérico. This makes the category easy to spot even if the front label doesn't say it.

steps.prompt: What does American oak typically give Rioja?
steps.explanation: American oak's lactones give these notes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva set minimum ageing
American oak gives vanilla and coconut; French oak is now common
